title: The Disposition Fee, Explained: What It Is and When It Disappears
description: Most leases include a charge for returning the car. Here is what it covers, how it is different from wear charges, and why buying can change whether you pay it.
body:
Of all the lease-end charges, the disposition fee is the one that surprises people most. It is in the contract, but it is easy to forget about three years later.

What the fee is for

A disposition fee is a flat amount your leasing company charges when you return the car. The stated reason is to cover the costs of taking the vehicle back: transport, cleaning, reconditioning, and arranging resale. Amounts vary by lessor and by contract, so check the number in your own paperwork rather than relying on a typical figure.

It is not the same as wear and tear

These are two separate charges and they can stack:

  • Disposition fee: a flat fee for processing a return.
  • Excess wear: charges for damage beyond what the contract defines as normal.
  • Excess mileage: a per-mile charge for miles above your allowance.

Someone with a spotless car and low mileage can still owe a disposition fee, simply for handing the car back.

When the fee may be waived or avoided

Because the fee is tied to processing a return, many contracts do not charge it when you buy the vehicle. Some contracts also reduce or waive it if you lease or buy another vehicle from the same brand. These terms are contract specific, so read the clause or ask directly. Do not assume a waiver applies; ask for confirmation that the fee is not part of your purchase price.

Questions to ask

  1. What is the disposition fee in my contract?
  2. Is it charged if I purchase the vehicle?
  3. Is it waived under any brand loyalty program?
  4. Is there a separate purchase option fee, and is it on top of the residual?

That last one is easy to confuse with the disposition fee. They are different charges with different triggers, and a contract may include one, both, or neither.

A quick way to compare returning and buying

Write two columns. Under "return," list the disposition fee, any excess mileage, any excess wear estimate, and the cost of finding a replacement vehicle. Under "buy," list the residual, any purchase option fee, sales tax, title and registration, and the cost of financing. The lower total is not automatically the winner, since you end up with a car in only one column, but it makes the tradeoff visible.

Get it in writing

If a representative tells you the fee will not apply, ask for a written payoff quote that shows the line items. A figure that appears on paper is much easier to rely on than one remembered from a call. The payoff call script has a short list of exactly what to request.
